docs.title: India's Informal Economy
docs.text: If you had to choose a single fact to characterise the Indian labour market, it would be this: the overwhelming majority of workers are informal. They work without written contracts, without social security, and without the legal protections that labour law nominally provides. Understanding informality is not a niche topic in Indian labour economics -- it is the central topic.

docs.title: Defining Informality
docs.text: Informality is a concept with multiple, overlapping definitions. The two most influential for India are the enterprise-based definition (informal sector) and the job-based definition (informal employment).

docs.title: The NCEUS Framework
docs.text:
The National Commission for Enterprises in the Unorganised Sector (NCEUS, 2007, 2009), chaired by Arjun Sengupta, provided the most widely cited definitions for the Indian context:

NCEUS Definitions

  • Informal sector (unorganised sector): All unincorporated private enterprises owned by individuals or households engaged in the sale or production of goods and services, operated on a proprietary or partnership basis, with fewer than 10 workers (or fewer than 20 if not using power).

  • Informal employment: Workers who do not receive employment-related social security benefits (provident fund, pension, gratuity, health care) from their employer, regardless of whether the enterprise is formal or informal.

The critical insight of the NCEUS framework is that these two dimensions are distinct. A worker can be in the formal sector but hold an informal job -- think of a contract cleaner working inside a large corporation without any benefits. The NCEUS estimated that in 2004-05, roughly 86 per cent of total employment was informal employment, while about 93 per cent of workers were in the informal sector. These numbers have changed only modestly since then.

docs.title: ILO Framework
docs.text: The International Labour Organization uses a similar two-dimensional framework. The 15th International Conference of Labour Statisticians (ICLS, 1993) defined the informal sector based on enterprise characteristics, while the 17th ICLS (2003) introduced the concept of informal employment based on the nature of the job. India's NCEUS definitions are broadly aligned with the ILO framework, though the employment-size thresholds differ from those used in other countries.

docs.title: Size and Structure
docs.text:
The numbers are staggering:

Indicator Estimate Informal sector employment (% of total) ~89% (PLFS 2023-24) Informal employment (% of total non-agricultural) ~75-80% Contribution to GDP ~50% (NCEUS estimate) Self-employment as share of total ~55-57% Casual labour as share of total ~22-24%

The Composition of Informality

The informal workforce is not homogeneous. It spans a wide spectrum:

  • Own-account workers (street vendors, small farmers, artisans) -- the largest group.
  • Contributing family workers (unpaid work on family farms or enterprises) -- disproportionately women.
  • Casual wage labourers (daily-wage construction workers, agricultural labourers) -- the most precarious group.
  • Regular informal workers (contract workers in factories, domestic workers) -- growing as formal firms outsource.

Each of these groups faces different constraints and responds differently to policy. Treating "the informal sector" as a monolith obscures more than it reveals.

docs.title: Characteristics of Informal Work
docs.text:
Informal employment in India is characterised by several features that distinguish it sharply from the textbook model of competitive labour markets:

Low and volatile earnings. Informal workers earn, on average, a fraction of what formal workers with similar observable characteristics earn. The NCEUS (2007) estimated that the average daily earnings of informal workers were roughly one-fourth those of formal workers. Earnings are also highly variable -- seasonal, weather-dependent, and subject to demand shocks.

Absence of social protection. The defining feature of informal employment is the lack of employer-provided social security. No provident fund, no health insurance, no pension, no paid leave, no gratuity. This means informal workers face old age, illness, and income shocks with almost no buffer.

Poor working conditions. Occupational health and safety standards are rarely observed. Construction workers, waste pickers, brick kiln labourers, and garment workers routinely face hazardous conditions without protective equipment or compensation for injuries. The compensating differentials framework (Chapter 5 of Borjas) predicts that such jobs should command a wage premium -- but in the Indian informal sector, the opposite often holds, because workers lack outside options.

Why Compensating Differentials Fail in the Informal Sector

The hedonic wage model assumes workers can freely choose between jobs with different risk-wage bundles. But if workers are constrained by caste, location, lack of education, or sheer desperation, they cannot "sort" into their preferred risk-wage combination. Instead, the worst jobs -- dangerous, dirty, and degrading -- are filled by the most disadvantaged workers at the lowest wages. This is the anti-compensating differential: bad jobs with bad pay, a pattern that the standard model cannot explain without incorporating labour market segmentation.

docs.title: Informal-Formal Linkages
docs.text:
The informal and formal sectors are not separate economies. They are deeply interlinked through subcontracting chains, labour supply relationships, and product market competition.

  • Subcontracting: Large formal-sector firms routinely outsource production steps to small informal enterprises. The garment industry is a classic example: a branded export house (formal) contracts cutting and stitching to workshops (informal) that employ casual workers at piece rates. The formal firm captures the value; the informal workers bear the risk.

  • Disguised wage employment: Many nominally "self-employed" workers in India are, in economic substance, dependent employees. Auto-rickshaw drivers who lease vehicles from fleet owners, delivery workers for platform companies, and home-based garment workers producing for a single contractor all fall into this grey zone.

  • Labour supply: The informal sector serves as a vast reservoir of labour for the formal sector during demand peaks, and absorbs workers ejected during downturns. This is not a smooth competitive adjustment -- it is a segmented market with large transition costs.

docs.title: Lewis Dual-Economy Model
docs.text:
Arthur Lewis (1954) proposed that developing economies have a traditional sector with unlimited supplies of labour at a subsistence wage, and a modern sector that draws workers from this pool as it accumulates capital. Growth occurs through the expansion of the modern sector, and the turning point arrives when the surplus labour in the traditional sector is exhausted and wages begin to rise.

Lewis Applied to India

India's informal sector can be thought of as Lewis's traditional sector -- a vast pool of underemployed workers available at low wages. The question is whether India has reached the Lewis turning point. Some scholars (e.g., Himanshu, 2011) have argued that rising real wages in rural India during 2007-2012 suggested an approaching turning point, though the subsequent slowdown in wage growth and persistent surplus labour cast doubt on this interpretation.

docs.title: Harris-Todaro Model
docs.text:
Harris and Todaro (1970) extended the Lewis framework by explaining why rural-urban migration continues even when urban unemployment is high. In their model, migrants compare the expected urban wage (formal sector wage multiplied by the probability of getting a formal job) with the certain rural wage. Equilibrium can feature persistent urban unemployment and an informal urban sector where workers queue for formal jobs.

The Harris-Todaro model maps well onto Indian cities. The sprawling urban informal sectors of Mumbai, Delhi, and Bangalore can be interpreted as waiting pools of workers hoping to transition into formal employment. Whether this "queue" interpretation or a "segmented markets" interpretation is correct remains debated.

docs.title: Segmented Labour Market Theory
docs.text:
A third perspective, associated with Doeringer and Piore (1971) and extended to developing countries by Fields (1975, 2005), argues that formal and informal labour markets are structurally segmented, not merely differentiated by worker productivity. Institutional barriers -- labour regulations, unionisation, minimum wages, hiring networks -- create rents in the formal sector that are not competed away. Informal workers are not merely less productive; they are rationed out of formal employment.

Evidence on Segmentation in India

Ramaswamy (2012, Indian Journal of Labour Economics) and Nath (2020) find evidence of significant formal-informal wage gaps in India that persist after controlling for education, experience, industry, and occupation. The residual gap -- often 30-60 per cent -- is consistent with segmentation rather than pure human capital differences. However, the direction of causality is difficult to establish, and unobserved heterogeneity remains a concern.

docs.title: Recent Trends: Has Formalisation Happened?
docs.text:
The question of whether India's economy is formalising has been hotly debated, particularly since 2016. Several policy interventions have been cited as potential drivers of formalisation:

  • Demonetisation (November 2016): The sudden withdrawal of high-denomination currency notes was partly justified as a blow against the "black economy," though its impact on actual formalisation is debated.

  • Goods and Services Tax (July 2017): By creating a unified indirect tax with an input tax credit chain, GST incentivised firms to register and transact formally. Early evidence suggests an increase in the number of GST-registered firms, though this does not automatically translate into formal employment.

  • Digital payments and UPI: The explosion of digital transactions has increased the traceability of economic activity, potentially nudging enterprises toward formal status.

  • EPFO enrolment data: The government has pointed to rising enrolments in the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) as evidence of formalisation. However, EPFO data conflate new formal jobs with formalisation of existing jobs and with multiple registrations by the same worker.

The Formalisation Debate

Abraham and co-authors (2023, Indian Journal of Labour Economics) argue that much of the apparent formalisation reflects a shift from self-employment to low-quality regular wage work -- "formalisation without security." Workers gain a regular employer but not social protection. Meanwhile, Ravi and co-authors (2019) suggest that firm registration has increased but the quality of formal jobs has not improved commensurately. The bottom line: formalisation in India is a process that is underway but remains shallow and incomplete.

docs.title: Policy Responses
docs.text:
India has pursued several policy strategies to address the vulnerabilities of informal workers:

e-Shram Portal (2021): A national database of unorganised workers, intended to serve as a single point of access to social welfare schemes. By early 2024, over 290 million workers had registered. The challenge is translating registration into actual benefit delivery.

PM-SYM (Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maan-dhan, 2019): A voluntary pension scheme for unorganised workers earning below Rs. 15,000 per month, providing Rs. 3,000 per month after age 60. Take-up has been lower than hoped -- fewer than 5 million enrollees by 2024 -- reflecting the classic problem of getting informal workers to commit to regular monthly contributions.

Code on Social Security, 2020: One of the four new labour codes that consolidate 29 existing laws. The Code extends social security provisions to gig workers, platform workers, and unorganised workers. However, the rules under the Code have not yet been fully notified by most states as of early 2026, and implementation remains uncertain.

PM Street Vendor's AtmaNirbhar Nidhi (PM SVANidhi, 2020): A micro-credit scheme for street vendors launched during COVID-19, providing working capital loans of up to Rs. 50,000 without collateral.

The Policy Trilemma

Formalising the informal sector faces a trilemma: (1) extending legal protections raises compliance costs for small firms, potentially destroying the very jobs it seeks to improve; (2) providing social security to workers outside formal employment relationships requires a financing mechanism that does not exist; and (3) registration and documentation requirements exclude the most vulnerable workers, who lack the literacy and digital access to navigate bureaucratic processes. Policy design must navigate all three horns simultaneously.

docs.title: Internal Migration in India
docs.text: India is a country of migrants. Yet for decades, internal migration remained statistically invisible, politically neglected, and academically understudied relative to its enormous scale. The textbook model of labour mobility -- developed primarily from the American experience of frictionless interstate movement -- breaks down spectacularly in a country where language, caste, welfare entitlements, and housing markets conspire to keep workers far less mobile than income differentials would predict. For students of labour economics, Indian internal migration is not merely an application of Labor Mobility theory -- it is a stress test of the standard model, revealing both its power and its limits.

docs.title: The Numbers
docs.text:
The most comprehensive count of internal migrants in India comes from the Census, which records place of last residence and place of birth. The 2011 Census enumerated approximately 450 million lifetime migrants -- persons residing in a place different from their place of birth. This makes India home to the largest internal migration flow in the world by absolute numbers.

Key Migration Statistics

Indicator Estimate Source Lifetime migrants (different place of birth) ~450 million Census 2011 Interstate migrants (last decade) ~60 million Economic Survey 2016-17 Annual interstate migration flow ~9 million Economic Survey 2016-17 Seasonal/circular migrants ~100 million (estimated) Various micro-studies Remittances to rural areas Significant but poorly measured NSS, CPHS

These numbers almost certainly undercount actual migration. The Census captures only those present at the destination on enumeration night. Short-term, seasonal, and circular migrants -- who shuttle between origin and destination over the course of a year -- are systematically missed.

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
The dominant stream is rural-to-urban migration, driven by the persistent wage gap between agricultural and non-agricultural employment. However, the composition is more varied than textbook treatments suggest:

  • Marriage migration is the single largest category in Census data, accounting for roughly half of all female migrants. This is primarily rural-to-rural movement associated with patrilocal marriage norms and is economically distinct from labour migration.
  • Labour migration dominates male interstate flows. The Economic Survey 2016-17, drawing on railway passenger data and other proxies, estimated that roughly 9 million people moved across state borders annually for work during 2011-2016.
  • Rural-to-rural migration for agricultural labour -- following the harvest calendar from state to state -- is substantial but almost invisible in official statistics.

docs.title: Key Corridors
docs.text:
Internal migration in India follows well-established corridors that reflect the geography of economic opportunity.

Major Migration Corridors

Origin states (labour surplus): Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha, Jharkhand, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal, Assam

Destination states (labour demand): Delhi, Maharashtra (Mumbai, Pune), Gujarat (Ahmedabad, Surat), Tamil Nadu (Chennai), Kerala, Karnataka (Bengaluru), Haryana, Punjab

Key corridors:

  • Bihar/UP to Delhi-NCR: The largest single corridor. Construction, manufacturing, domestic work, rickshaw-pulling, and street vending absorb millions of workers from the Gangetic plains.
  • Bihar/UP to Mumbai and Gujarat: Textile mills in Surat, diamond polishing in Gujarat, and Mumbai's vast service economy draw workers from eastern UP and Bihar.
  • Odisha/Jharkhand to Kerala and Tamil Nadu: Plantation labour, construction, and fishing industries in southern states recruit heavily from eastern India. The wage differential is particularly stark -- casual daily wages in Kerala can be two to three times those in Odisha.
  • Northeast to Delhi and Bengaluru: Young workers from Assam, Manipur, Mizoram, and Nagaland migrate to metropolitan cities, often into the hospitality, retail, and beauty services sectors. They face distinctive challenges including racial discrimination and cultural dislocation.
  • Rajasthan to Gujarat: Short-distance seasonal migration for salt pans, cotton harvesting, and brick kilns.

These corridors are remarkably persistent over time, sustained by network effects: once a few pioneers from a village establish themselves at a destination, information and assistance flow back, lowering the migration cost for subsequent movers.

docs.title: Migration as Human Capital Investment
docs.text:
The standard economic model of migration, originating with Sjaastad (1962), treats the decision to migrate as an investment in human capital. A worker compares the present value of lifetime earnings at the destination against those at the origin, net of migration costs:

$$ \text{Migrate if } \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{w_d(t) - w_o(t)}{(1+r)^t} > C $$

where $w_d(t)$ and $w_o(t)$ are destination and origin earnings, $r$ is the discount rate, $T$ is the remaining working life, and $C$ encompasses direct moving costs plus psychic costs of separation from family and community. In the Indian context, $C$ is exceptionally high for reasons discussed below, which explains why migration rates are lower than the wage gap alone would predict.

docs.title: The Roy Model and Self-Selection
docs.text:
Who migrates? The Roy model (applied to migration by Borjas, 1987) predicts that the selection pattern depends on the return to skill in origin and destination. If the destination rewards skill more than the origin (wider wage distribution), migrants will be positively selected -- the most able workers move. If the origin rewards skill more, migrants will be negatively selected.

Self-Selection in Indian Migration

The Indian evidence suggests a complex pattern. Positively selected migration characterises the high-skill stream: engineers moving from tier-2 cities to Bengaluru, doctors moving to metro hospitals, IIT graduates moving to the US. But the bulk of low-skill interstate migration appears to involve workers from the lower-middle of the origin skill distribution -- not the very poorest (who cannot afford to move) nor the well-off (who have adequate local opportunities). This is consistent with the model when migration costs are high: only those whose expected gain exceeds the substantial cost threshold will move, which excludes both tails of the distribution.

Munshi and Rosenzweig (2016, Quarterly Journal of Economics) provide micro-evidence that caste-based insurance networks discourage out-migration of male members, creating a selection pattern driven by social structure rather than purely by individual returns to skill.

docs.title: Barriers to Migration
docs.text: India's internal migration rate is anomalously low given its income differentials. Kone, Liu, Mattoo, Ozden, and Piracha (2018) provide the most systematic cross-country comparison, finding that India's interstate migration rate is roughly one-third of what a standard gravity model -- calibrated on cross-country data with similar income gaps, population sizes, and distances -- would predict. Several barriers explain this gap.

docs.title: Language Fragmentation
docs.text: India has 22 scheduled languages and hundreds of dialects. A worker from Bihar (Hindi) moving to Tamil Nadu (Tamil) or Kerala (Malayalam) faces a language barrier with no parallel in the United States or China. Language affects access to information, negotiation of wages, interaction with authorities, and social integration. This is not merely a convenience issue -- it is an economic cost that enters directly into the migration cost term $C$ in the investment model.

docs.title: Caste and Kinship Networks
docs.text:
Caste Networks as Migration Barriers

Munshi and Rosenzweig (2016, Quarterly Journal of Economics) show that caste-based mutual insurance networks -- which provide informal social protection against income shocks in the origin village -- actively discourage spatial mobility. Male members of well-functioning jati networks are less likely to migrate, because migration would sever their access to the network's insurance function and reduce the network's risk-pooling capacity. The key insight is that caste networks are geographically bounded: they provide insurance only in the local area. A worker who migrates loses this safety net without gaining a formal substitute at the destination. This creates a migration penalty that is invisible in standard economic models but quantitatively large.

docs.title: Non-Portability of Welfare Entitlements
docs.text:
India's social protection architecture is deeply place-based. The Public Distribution System (PDS) -- which provides subsidised food grain to roughly 800 million people -- is tied to ration cards issued at the place of residence. A migrant worker from Bihar working on a construction site in Gujarat could not, until recently, use their ration card in Gujarat. Similarly, access to public housing, school admissions, and health services is typically tied to domicile status.

The Portability Problem

The non-portability of entitlements acts as an implicit tax on migration. A worker who moves loses access to subsidised food, children's school places, and potential MGNREGA employment at home. The Aadhaar-based identity system was expected to solve this by enabling portable, individual-level entitlements. In practice, Aadhaar has facilitated financial inclusion but has not fully solved the portability problem -- PDS portability through the One Nation One Ration Card (ONORC) scheme was announced in 2019 but remained incompletely implemented when the COVID-19 crisis exposed its gaps.

docs.title: Housing and Informal Settlement
docs.text: Migrant workers in Indian cities overwhelmingly live in informal housing -- slum clusters, construction-site dormitories, shared rooms with shift-sleeping arrangements, or pavement dwellings. Formal rental housing markets are thin and exclusionary (landlords discriminate by religion, caste, region of origin, and dietary habits). The absence of affordable housing at the destination raises $C$ substantially and helps explain why so much Indian migration is temporary and circular rather than permanent.

docs.title: Sons-of-the-Soil Politics
docs.text: Political movements targeting migrants have recurred across Indian states. The Shiv Sena in Maharashtra (targeting South Indians in the 1960s, then North Indians from the 1990s onward), demands for domicile-based job quotas in Jharkhand, Assam, and Haryana, and periodic violence against migrant workers in the Northeast all raise the perceived risk and psychic cost of migration. These political barriers have no close analogue in the US textbook model.

docs.title: Seasonal and Circular Migration
docs.text:
A distinctive feature of Indian internal migration is the prevalence of seasonal and circular movement -- workers who migrate for part of the year and return to their home villages for the rest. This pattern is driven by the agricultural calendar, the seasonal nature of demand in key industries, and the desire to maintain village-based entitlements and social ties.

Key Sectors Using Seasonal Migrant Labour

  • Construction: India's largest employer of seasonal migrants. Workers from Bihar, Odisha, Jharkhand, and Chhattisgarh staff construction sites across urban India. They are recruited through labour contractors (thekedars) who advance wages, arrange transport, and often exercise considerable control over working conditions.
  • Brick kilns: An estimated 10-15 million workers, many from Odisha and Chhattisgarh, spend 6-8 months per year moulding bricks in kilns across western and southern India. Families migrate together, and children frequently work alongside parents. Piece-rate payment is universal.
  • Sugarcane harvesting: In Maharashtra, roughly 1 million workers -- predominantly from the Marathwada drought belt -- migrate annually for the October-March sugarcane cutting season. They are recruited by mukadams (contractors) who advance loans before the season, creating debt-bondage dynamics.
  • Salt pans: Workers from Rajasthan and Kutch spend months at coastal salt pans under extreme conditions.
  • Domestic work: Increasingly, young women from Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, and tribal areas of West Bengal migrate to Delhi and other metros as domestic workers, often through placement agencies with limited accountability.

Deshingkar and Akter (2009) provide the most comprehensive overview of seasonal migration patterns, documenting how the contractor system -- rather than individual decision-making -- mediates much of this movement. The textbook model of the atomistic individual comparing wage differentials understates the role of intermediaries who recruit, transport, and supervise migrant labour in exchange for a share of their wages.

Women's participation in seasonal migration is substantial but varies by sector. In brick kilns and sugarcane harvesting, entire families migrate. In construction, male-dominated crews are more common, though women increasingly participate in urban construction. In domestic work, the flow is overwhelmingly female.

docs.title: MGNREGA and Migration
docs.text:
NREGA Reduces Seasonal Out-Migration

Imbert and Papp (2015, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics) provide rigorous evidence that MGNREGA reduced seasonal out-migration from rural areas. Using the programme's phased rollout across districts as a natural experiment, they find that NREGA districts experienced approximately a 10 per cent decline in temporary out-migration during the agricultural lean season. The mechanism is the reservation wage channel: by providing guaranteed employment at the NREGA wage in the home village, the programme raised the opportunity cost of migrating. Workers who would otherwise have endured the costs of seasonal migration to urban construction sites or brick kilns chose instead to work on NREGA projects locally.

This is a direct application of the migration investment model: NREGA raised $w_o(t)$ (the origin wage), reducing the net gain from migration below the cost threshold $C$ for marginal migrants. See the NREGA essay for a detailed treatment of the programme's labour market effects.

The welfare implications of reduced migration are ambiguous. If NREGA enables workers to avoid exploitative seasonal work under harsh conditions, the welfare gain is clear. But if it discourages migration that would yield higher lifetime earnings, the long-run human capital consequences are less favourable. The evidence suggests that NREGA primarily reduces distress migration -- movement undertaken not as a productive investment but as a survival strategy during the lean season -- which is welfare-improving on net.

docs.title: The COVID-19 Migrant Crisis
docs.text: The nationwide lockdown announced on 24 March 2020, with four hours' notice, exposed the invisibility of India's migrant workforce with devastating clarity.

docs.title: The Reverse Migration Wave
docs.text:
With factories, construction sites, and markets shuttered overnight, an estimated 10-12 million migrant workers attempted to return to their home villages. Lacking transport (railways and inter-state buses were suspended), savings (most had fewer than two weeks' worth), and housing (dormitories were closed), thousands began walking hundreds of kilometres along national highways. Images of families with children walking on expressways became the defining visual of India's pandemic experience.

What the Crisis Revealed

The migrant crisis exposed multiple, compounding policy failures:

  • No data: The government did not know how many migrant workers were in which cities. There was no registry, no database, no count. The Census (last conducted in 2011) was a decade old. The PLFS does not track short-term migrants effectively.
  • No portability: Migrants could not access PDS rations at their work location. The ONORC scheme existed on paper but was not operational in most states.
  • No housing: Migrant workers in informal housing had no tenure security. When work stopped, they were evicted or unable to pay rent.
  • No social protection: MGNREGA is a rural programme. Urban migrant workers had no equivalent safety net. No unemployment insurance, no emergency cash transfer mechanism reached them promptly.
  • No coordination: The response was fragmented across central, state, and local governments, with origin and destination states blaming each other.

Srivastava (2020) provides an early and comprehensive account of the crisis, documenting the scale of reverse migration, the inadequacy of the policy response, and the structural neglect of migrant workers in Indian social policy.

docs.title: Aftermath
docs.text:
The crisis had lasting consequences. Many workers who returned home did not immediately re-migrate, depressing urban labour supply in construction and manufacturing through 2020 and into 2021. MGNREGA demand spiked to record levels as returnees sought rural employment. Some workers reported a permanent change in their migration calculus -- the trauma of the lockdown experience raised the psychic cost $C$ in their migration decision, at least temporarily.

The crisis also forced policy attention. The e-Shram portal, launched in 2021, aimed to create a national database of unorganised workers, including migrants, with Aadhaar-linked registration. By 2023, over 290 million workers had registered, though the portal's utility for delivering actual benefits remains limited.

docs.title: Legislative Framework
docs.text:
The Interstate Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979 was the primary legislation governing interstate labour migration. It required contractors to register migrant workers, provide displacement allowance, and ensure basic amenities. In practice, enforcement was negligible -- the vast majority of migrant workers had never heard of the Act, and labour inspectorates lacked the capacity to monitor compliance.

The 1979 Act was subsumed into the Code on Social Security, 2020, one of four labour codes that consolidated 29 central labour laws. The Code includes provisions for a national database of unorganised workers, portability of welfare benefits, and the establishment of a Social Security Fund for gig and platform workers. The labour codes have been passed by Parliament but are yet to be fully implemented, with states required to frame rules for operationalisation.

docs.title: Recent Initiatives
docs.text:
Key Policy Responses

  • One Nation One Ration Card (ONORC): Enables PDS beneficiaries to draw their entitled ration from any Fair Price Shop in the country using Aadhaar-linked biometric authentication. Operational in all 36 states and Union Territories as of 2024. A significant step toward entitlement portability, though awareness among migrants remains low.
  • e-Shram Portal: A centralised database of unorganised and migrant workers. Provides a Universal Account Number (UAN) linked to Aadhaar. Intended as the infrastructure for future benefit delivery.
  • PM-SVANidhi (Street Vendor Scheme): Micro-credit for street vendors, many of whom are migrants, launched during the COVID-19 recovery.
  • Ayushman Bharat portability: Health insurance under PM-JAY is technically portable, but operational portability at hospitals across states is uneven.

docs.title: What Remains Missing
docs.text: Despite these initiatives, the fundamental challenge persists: Indian policy is designed around sedentary populations, while the economy depends on mobile labour. A comprehensive migration policy would require portable entitlements across all welfare programmes, enforceable standards for migrant worker housing, urban planning that acknowledges (rather than criminalises) migrant settlement, and a reliable real-time data system that tracks migration flows. India currently has none of these at scale.

docs.title: NREGA: India's Employment Guarantee
docs.text: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA, commonly called NREGA) is one of the most ambitious social protection programmes in the world. Enacted in 2005, it guarantees 100 days of unskilled manual wage employment per year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer to do such work. For students of labour economics, NREGA is not merely a welfare programme -- it is a labour market intervention that directly alters reservation wages, rural wage dynamics, migration patterns, and the equilibrium distribution of employment. It is a living experiment in the textbook models of Chapters 2, 4, and 11.

docs.title: The Legal Guarantee
docs.text:
NREGA is unique among workfare programmes because it provides a legal right to employment. If a rural household demands work and the local government (gram panchayat) fails to provide it within 15 days, the household is entitled to an unemployment allowance. This demand-driven design distinguishes NREGA from supply-driven programmes where the government decides when and where to create jobs.

Key Design Features

Feature Detail Eligibility Any rural household (adult members willing to do unskilled manual work) Entitlement 100 days of guaranteed employment per household per financial year Wage State-specific NREGA wage rate (notified annually; ranges from Rs. 234 to Rs. 374 per day across states in 2024-25) Works Water conservation, drought proofing, rural connectivity, land development, flood control Gender At least one-third of workers must be women (actual share has exceeded 50% nationally) Childcare If 5 or more children under 6 are at a worksite, a crèche must be provided Transparency All expenditures are publicly available through the MIS portal (nrega.nic.in) Implementation Gram panchayats plan and execute works; funds flow from central to state to district to GP

docs.title: Self-Targeting Mechanism
docs.text:
Self-Targeting: An Elegant Design

NREGA uses a self-targeting mechanism: the programme offers hard manual labour at a relatively low wage. This means that only those who truly need the work will demand it. Better-off workers with higher reservation wages voluntarily opt out. In the textbook framework:

  • A worker participates in NREGA if and only if their market wage ( w_m ) is less than the NREGA wage ( w_N ):

[ \text{Participate if } w_m < w_N ]

  • Workers whose skills command a market wage above ( w_N ) self-select out of the programme.

This elegantly avoids the need for costly means testing (verifying who is "poor enough" to qualify). The work requirement itself filters out non-poor applicants. This is the classic workfare vs. welfare distinction that the labour supply model in Chapter 2 illuminates.

docs.title: Labour Market Effects
docs.text: NREGA's effects on the rural labour market have been extensively studied and are among the best-documented programme impacts in development economics.

docs.title: The Reservation Wage Floor
docs.text:
The most fundamental effect of NREGA is that it sets a floor on the reservation wage of rural workers. Before NREGA, a casual agricultural labourer in a slack season had no outside option -- accept whatever wage the local employer offers, or starve. With NREGA, the same worker can refuse wages below the NREGA rate, because they have an alternative source of employment.

NREGA as a Reservation Wage Shifter

In the Chapter 2 framework, the reservation wage ( w^* ) is the minimum wage at which a worker is willing to supply labour. NREGA effectively sets:

[ w^ = \max(w^_{\text{original}}, w_N) ]

For workers whose original reservation wage was below the NREGA wage, the programme raises ( w^ ) to ( w_N ). This shifts the labour supply curve to the left (at any wage below ( w_N ), fewer workers are available to private employers), which puts upward pressure on private-sector wages*. This is precisely what the empirical evidence finds.

docs.title: Impact on Rural Wages
docs.text:
Wages: The Key Finding

Imbert and Papp (2015, American Economic Review) provide the most rigorous evidence on NREGA's wage effects. Using a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits the phased rollout of NREGA across districts (Phase 1 in 2006, Phase 2 in 2007, Phase 3 in 2008), they find:

  • NREGA raised casual wages in the private sector by approximately 4.7 per cent during the agricultural lean season.
  • The effect was concentrated in the dry season, when NREGA activity peaks and private agricultural labour demand is low.
  • The effect was larger in districts with better NREGA implementation (measured by actual employment generated).
  • The wage increase benefited not only NREGA participants but all casual workers in treated districts -- a general equilibrium effect through the labour market.

This is a clean example of the competitive equilibrium model (Chapter 4): a positive supply shock to one employer (the government) tightens the labour market for other employers, raising the equilibrium wage for all.

docs.title: Impact on Migration
docs.text:
NREGA was also expected to reduce distress migration by providing employment in the home village. The evidence on this is more nuanced:

  • Imbert and Papp (2015) find that NREGA reduced temporary out-migration from rural areas during the lean season by about 10 per cent. Workers who would have migrated to urban construction sites or brick kilns stayed home to work on NREGA projects.

  • Zimmermann (2020, Journal of Labor Economics) examines the migration channel more carefully and finds that NREGA induced a reallocation of labour from the private to the public sector during the lean season, but did not significantly reduce permanent migration. Seasonal and circular migration, however, declined.

NREGA and the Harris-Todaro Model

NREGA complicates the standard Harris-Todaro framework. In that model, rural workers migrate to urban areas when the expected urban wage exceeds the certain rural wage. NREGA raises the "certain rural wage" (by providing guaranteed employment at ( w_N )), which should reduce migration. In equilibrium:

[ w_N + \text{NREGA employment probability} \times w_N > w_R \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{Migration falls} ]

The phased-rollout evidence is broadly consistent with this prediction, at least for seasonal migration.

docs.title: Impact on Agricultural Labour Markets
docs.text:
NREGA's wage effects had ripple consequences for agricultural employers. Several studies document that:

  • Landowners responded to higher wages by shifting toward mechanisation (tractors, harvesters) and less labour-intensive crops. Berg, Bhatt, and"; show evidence of this substitution effect in parts of Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh.

  • Labour rationing during peak season became a complaint of farmers in states with high NREGA activity, though this claim is disputed -- NREGA activity falls sharply during the peak agricultural season (kharif sowing/harvest), suggesting complementarity rather than conflict.

docs.title: Key Research Papers
docs.text:
Beyond Imbert and Papp, several other major studies have shaped our understanding of NREGA:

Muralidharan, Niehaus, and Sukhtankar (2023, American Economic Review) study the effect of biometric smartcard-based payments for NREGA in Andhra Pradesh. They find that improving the payment system (reducing delays and leakage) increased the effective wage received by workers, increased NREGA participation, and raised private-sector casual wages through the reservation wage channel. This paper demonstrates that programme design details -- how workers are paid, not just how much -- have first-order labour market effects.

Zimmermann (2020, Journal of Labor Economics) uses the phased rollout and finds that NREGA raised private-sector wages by shifting labour supply. She emphasises the general equilibrium nature of the effect: even non-participants benefit from tighter labour markets.

Klonner and Oldiges (2014) find that NREGA reduced rural poverty in early-phase districts, consistent with the programme's role as an income floor.

Dutta, Murgai, Ravallion, and van de Walle (2012, World Bank Economic Review) provide a more cautious assessment, showing that rationing is severe -- many households that demand NREGA work do not receive it, and those who do often get far fewer than 100 days.

docs.title: Implementation Challenges
docs.text: The gap between NREGA's elegant design and its on-the-ground reality is substantial.

docs.title: Delayed Payments
docs.text:
The Payment Problem

Perhaps the most persistent implementation failure is delayed wage payments. NREGA mandates payment within 15 days of work completion, but studies have found average delays of 30-90 days in many states. Delayed payments effectively reduce the present value of the NREGA wage, discouraging participation by precisely the poorest workers who cannot afford to wait. Khera (2011, Economic and Political Weekly) documents cases where workers waited months for payment, defeating the programme's purpose as a timely safety net. The shift to direct bank transfers and Aadhaar-linked payments has improved timeliness in some states, but the problem persists in others.

docs.title: Rationing and Unmet Demand
docs.text: Despite the legal guarantee of 100 days, the average number of days worked per household nationally has been around 45-50 days in recent years. Many households receive zero days. This rationing reflects both supply-side constraints (insufficient budget allocation, slow administrative processes) and local political economy factors (panchayat leaders prioritising certain areas or groups).

docs.title: Corruption and Leakage
docs.text:
NREGA is not immune to the governance challenges that afflict Indian public programmes. Common problems include:

  • Ghost workers: Fictitious names on muster rolls, with wages siphoned by officials.
  • Inflated material expenditures: Claiming higher-than-actual costs for materials (cement, gravel), leaving less for wages.
  • Measurement fraud: Recording fewer days worked than actually performed, or recording work that was never done.

Social audits -- a mandatory feature of NREGA -- have been most effective in Andhra Pradesh/Telangana, where an independent state-level agency conducts audits. In most other states, social audit capacity is weak.

docs.title: Quality of Assets
docs.text: NREGA creates durable assets -- ponds, roads, irrigation channels, land levelling -- in addition to providing employment. The quality of these assets has been variable. Some studies (Mani et al., 2020; Shah and Mehta, 2020) find that well-planned NREGA works have improved agricultural productivity and water availability. Others find hastily constructed works that deteriorate within a year.

docs.title: Gender and NREGA
docs.text:
One of NREGA's notable successes is high female participation:

Women in NREGA

Nationally, women constitute over 55 per cent of NREGA person-days worked, far exceeding the statutory minimum of one-third. In states like Kerala and Tamil Nadu, female participation exceeds 80 per cent. This is significant because:

  1. NREGA offers work close to home, which reduces the mobility constraint that limits women's access to other employment.
  2. NREGA wages are the same for men and women by law, which means women receive the full notified wage rather than the gender-discounted wage prevalent in private agricultural labour markets.
  3. NREGA may increase women's bargaining power within households by providing an independent source of income. Afridi, Mukhopadhyay, and Sahoo (2016, Journal of Development Economics) find evidence that NREGA employment is associated with improved nutrition among children in participant households, consistent with women directing NREGA income toward food.

However, women also face specific challenges: they are more likely to receive delayed payments, less likely to receive unemployment allowance when work is not provided, and often perform the most labour-intensive tasks (earth-moving, water-carrying).

docs.title: NREGA in the COVID-19 Crisis
docs.text:
NREGA played a crucial role during the COVID-19 pandemic:

  • During the nationwide lockdown (March-June 2020), millions of migrant workers returned to rural areas (see the Migration essay). NREGA was one of the few programmes that could absorb this sudden influx of labour.
  • Demand for NREGA spiked: in FY 2020-21, NREGA generated 389 crore person-days of employment -- the highest since its inception.
  • The government increased the NREGA wage by Rs. 20 and raised the budget allocation from Rs. 61,500 crore to over Rs. 1,11,000 crore during the crisis year.
  • NREGA's demand-driven design proved its value: unlike supply-driven programmes that could not scale quickly, NREGA could accommodate rising demand (albeit with delays and rationing).

docs.title: Fiscal Cost and Sustainability
docs.text:
NREGA is a significant fiscal commitment. The annual budget allocation has typically been Rs. 60,000-90,000 crore (approximately USD 7-11 billion), making it one of India's largest social protection programmes. Critics argue that:

  • The programme crowds out more productive public investment.
  • The fiscal cost is high relative to the poverty reduction achieved.
  • The work created has limited productivity impact relative to direct cash transfers.

Supporters counter that:

  • NREGA's insurance function (providing income during shocks) is worth more than the direct wage payment, because it prevents asset depletion and distress migration.
  • The asset creation component generates returns that are difficult to capture in standard cost-benefit analysis.
  • The general equilibrium wage effects benefit all rural casual workers, not just programme participants.

NREGA vs. Cash Transfers: A Textbook Debate

The comparison between NREGA (in-kind transfer of employment) and unconditional cash transfers maps directly onto the Chapter 2 analysis of in-kind vs. cash transfers. The labour supply model predicts that cash transfers are weakly preferred by recipients (they can always choose to work if they want to). The argument for NREGA-style workfare is threefold: (1) self-targeting reduces fiscal cost by screening out the non-poor; (2) the work requirement may be politically sustainable in ways that cash transfers are not; (3) the asset creation component provides public goods. The optimal design depends on the relative importance of these factors, which is ultimately an empirical question.

docs.title: Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) -- A Student's Guide
docs.text: The Periodic Labour Force Survey is India's most important source of labour market statistics. If you want to make any empirical claim about Indian employment, wages, or unemployment, the PLFS is almost certainly the dataset you will turn to first. This guide introduces the survey, explains its core concepts, and helps you read and interpret PLFS annual reports.

docs.title: What is the PLFS?
docs.text:
The PLFS is a nationwide household survey conducted by the National Statistical Office (NSO), which is part of the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI). It was launched in 2017-18 as a successor to the quinquennial Employment-Unemployment Surveys (EUS) that the NSO had conducted since the 1970s under the National Sample Survey (NSS) framework.

Why the PLFS Matters

Before 2017-18, India's official employment data came once every five years (the last EUS was in 2011-12). The PLFS was introduced to provide annual estimates of labour force indicators and, for urban areas, quarterly estimates. This was a major upgrade in the timeliness of India's labour statistics.

The PLFS follows a rotational panel design in urban areas: the urban sample is divided into four panels, each surveyed for four consecutive quarters, with one panel rotating out each quarter. This means 75 per cent of the urban sample is common between two consecutive quarters, allowing for more reliable estimation of quarter-on-quarter changes. The rural sample, by contrast, is surveyed only once during the annual survey period (July to June for earlier rounds; January to December from PLFS 2024 onward).

The survey covers the entire territory of India except a few inaccessible areas in Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Sample sizes are large: the PLFS 2023-24, for instance, covered approximately 1,01,655 households and over 4,00,000 individuals.

docs.title: Key Concepts: Activity Status
docs.text: The most important conceptual framework in the PLFS is the classification of individuals by activity status -- that is, what they were doing during a specified reference period. The PLFS collects activity status using three different reference periods, each yielding a different picture of the labour market.

docs.title: Usual Principal Status (UPS)
docs.text:
• Reference period: 365 days preceding the survey date.
  • Definition: The activity on which a person spent the major part (i.e., more than 6 months) of the reference year.
  • Use: Gives a broad, structural picture of employment. A person is classified as employed, unemployed, or out of the labour force based on what they did for most of the year.

docs.title: Usual Principal and Subsidiary Status (UPSS)
docs.text:
• Reference period: 365 days preceding the survey date.
  • Definition: Extends UPS by adding a subsidiary activity for persons who were classified as unemployed or out of the labour force under UPS, but who pursued some economic activity for at least 30 days during the reference year.
  • Use: The most commonly cited activity status in PLFS reports. UPSS captures a broader set of workers than UPS alone, because it picks up people whose primary status is non-working but who did some work on the side.

Why UPSS Matters for Measurement

Consider a woman who spends most of the year on domestic duties but works on the family farm for two months during the harvest season. Under UPS, she is classified as "not in the labour force." Under UPSS, she is classified as employed (subsidiary status). This distinction is crucial for understanding female LFPR in India, where a large share of women's work is seasonal or part-time.

docs.title: Current Weekly Status (CWS)
docs.text:
• Reference period: 7 days preceding the survey date.
  • Definition: A person is classified as employed if they pursued any economic activity for at least one hour on any day during the reference week.
  • Use: Provides a shorter-term snapshot. CWS estimates of unemployment are typically higher than UPSS estimates, because they capture people who may be employed for most of the year but happen to be without work in the reference week.

docs.title: Current Daily Status (CDS)
docs.text:
• Reference period: Each day of the 7 days preceding the survey date.
  • Definition: Activity status is determined for each day of the reference week (each day assigned one of two "half-day" slots). A person-day is the unit of measurement.
  • Use: Gives the most granular picture and captures underemployment effectively. CDS unemployment rates are the highest among the three measures because they pick up even partial-week idleness.

Comparing the Three Measures (PLFS 2023-24)

Measure Unemployment Rate UPSS ~3.2% CWS ~4.1% CDS ~5.0%

The gap between these rates reflects the extent of intermittent and seasonal unemployment that UPSS smooths over. When reading PLFS reports, always check which definition is being used -- headlines citing different activity statuses can paint very different pictures of the same labour market.

docs.title: Core Labour Market Indicators
docs.text:
The PLFS reports several key indicators. Here are the definitions you need:

Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR): The proportion of the population (aged 15 years and above) that is either employed or unemployed (i.e., seeking or available for work).

[ \text{LFPR} = \frac{\text{Labour Force (Employed + Unemployed)}}{\text{Population aged 15+}} \times 100 ]

Worker Population Ratio (WPR): The proportion of the population (aged 15+) that is employed.

[ \text{WPR} = \frac{\text{Employed}}{\text{Population aged 15+}} \times 100 ]

Unemployment Rate (UR): The proportion of the labour force that is unemployed.

[ \text{UR} = \frac{\text{Unemployed}}{\text{Labour Force}} \times 100 ]

Note that the PLFS often reports these for persons aged 15 and above as well as for all ages (including children aged 5-14, for subsidiary activities). The standard international practice -- and what you should use in your assignments -- is the 15+ definition.

docs.title: Key Variables and Codes
docs.text:
When working with PLFS unit-level data, you will encounter the following important variables:

Variable Description Key Codes NIC (National Industrial Classification) Industry of employment 2-digit and 5-digit codes per NIC-2008 NCO (National Classification of Occupations) Occupation 2-digit and 3-digit codes per NCO-2004 Status Code Activity status 11-51 = employed; 81 = unemployed (sought); 91-98 = not in labour force Type of Enterprise Formal/informal sector proxy Proprietary, partnership, employer categories Social Group Caste category ST = 1, SC = 2, OBC = 3, Others = 9 Wage/Earnings Weekly earnings for CWS Reported in rupees for regular/casual workers Education Level Highest completed level Coded 01 (not literate) through 13 (postgraduate and above)

Working with PLFS Microdata

PLFS unit-level data can be downloaded from the MoSPI website after registration. The data arrives as fixed-width text files (.TXT) with separate record layouts for household and person records. You will need to apply the NSO's provided layout to read these into Stata or Python. Sample Stata workflow:

* Read person-level records using NSO layout
infix using plfs_person_layout.dct, using(plfs_person.txt)
* Generate employment dummy
gen employed = inrange(status_code, 11, 51)
* Compute LFPR
gen in_lf = inrange(status_code, 11, 82)

docs.title: How to Read PLFS Annual Reports
docs.text:
The NSO publishes annual PLFS reports (typically with a lag of about one year). Here is a roadmap for navigating them:

  1. Executive Summary (first few pages): Key headline indicators -- LFPR, WPR, UR -- by UPSS and CWS, separately for rural/urban and male/female.

  2. Statement Tables: Numbered tables (e.g., Statement 4, Statement 5) are the main data source. These provide cross-tabulations by state, age group, education level, social group, industry, and occupation. Learn to cite these by Statement number.

  3. Appendix Tables: More detailed breakdowns, often by individual states.

  4. Methodology Section: Explains sample design, weighting procedures, and response rates. Always check this when doing research, because PLFS has changed its reference period (from July-June to January-December starting in 2024), and comparability across rounds requires care.

Watch for Breaks in Series

The PLFS underwent a significant methodological change in 2024, shifting from a July-June survey period to a January-December calendar year. This means direct comparisons between PLFS 2022-23 and PLFS 2024 require caution. Additionally, the COVID year (2020-21) had a truncated survey period due to lockdowns. Always flag these breaks when presenting time-series data.

docs.title: Limitations and Caveats
docs.text:
No survey is perfect, and the PLFS has several known limitations that you should keep in mind:

  • Undercounting of women's work: Despite improvements over the old EUS, the PLFS still relies on a single household informant in many cases, and domestic/care work is systematically undercounted. The UPSS activity-status approach has been criticised for missing the episodic and part-time nature of much of women's employment.

  • No income data for self-employed: The PLFS collects earnings data only for regular wage/salaried and casual workers. The roughly 55 per cent of workers who are self-employed do not report earnings in the PLFS. This is a major limitation for wage analysis.

  • Urban bias in quarterly estimates: Quarterly bulletins cover only urban areas, so short-term trends in rural labour markets are invisible between annual rounds.

  • Panel attrition: The rotational panel in urban areas suffers from attrition, particularly among migrants and mobile populations -- precisely the groups of most interest for studying labour market dynamics.

  • Comparability with NSS-EUS: Although the PLFS uses the same conceptual framework as the old EUS rounds, differences in questionnaire design, sample design, and reference periods mean that pre-2017 and post-2017 series are not directly comparable without adjustments.

docs.title: Useful Links
docs.text:
• PLFS Annual Reports: MoSPI PLFS page -- official annual reports and quarterly bulletins.
  • Unit-Level Data: Available through the MoSPI microdata portal after free registration.
  • NSO Documentation: Concepts and definitions aligned with ILO standards are described in the NSO's Sources and Methods volume.
  • ILO ILOSTAT: ilostat.ilo.org -- for cross-country comparisons using harmonised definitions.

Bottom Line for Students

The PLFS is your go-to source for Indian labour market data. When you cite an employment or unemployment figure for India, always specify: (1) the PLFS round (e.g., 2023-24), (2) the activity status (UPSS, CWS, or CDS), (3) the age group (15+ or all ages), and (4) whether the figure is for rural, urban, or all-India. Failing to specify these will make your analysis ambiguous.

This guide is based on PLFS reports and methodology documents published by MoSPI/NSO. For the latest data, always consult the official MoSPI website.

docs.title: Stata for Labour Economics
docs.text: A practical guide to using Stata for empirical analysis in ECON207. This page covers the essentials you need for the course -- from navigating the interface to running Mincer regressions on Indian labour market data.

docs.title: Why Stata?
docs.text:
Stata is the industry-standard software for applied microeconometrics and labour economics research. The vast majority of published empirical papers in labour economics -- from Card and Krueger's minimum wage study to Oaxaca-Blinder wage decompositions -- were produced in Stata. Learning Stata is not just a course requirement; it is a transferable skill for any career in economic research, policy analysis, or data-driven consulting.

Why Stata for this course specifically?

  • FLAME lab access. Stata is installed on all Economics Lab machines. You do not need to purchase a personal license (though student licenses are affordable).
  • Reproducibility. Stata do-files create a permanent record of every step in your analysis, from data cleaning to final tables. This is essential for the group assignments.
  • Ecosystem. The Stata community has developed thousands of user-written commands for labour economics tasks (decompositions, matching estimators, instrumental variables diagnostics).

Your first command

Open Stata, type the following in the Command window, and press Enter:

display "Hello, Labour Economics!"

If you see the output, you are ready to go.

docs.title: Getting Started: The Stata Interface
docs.text:
When you open Stata, you will see five main areas:

Panel Purpose Command window Type individual commands here Results window Output from commands appears here Variables window Lists all variables in the current dataset Properties window Shows variable labels, types, and formats Review window History of commands you have run (click to re-run)

docs.title: Command Window vs. Do-File
docs.text:
You can run Stata commands in two ways:

  1. Interactively -- type commands one at a time in the Command window. Good for exploration.
  2. Via a do-file -- write a script containing multiple commands, then execute it. This is what you should use for assignments.

Creating a do-file

Go to File > New > Do-file (or press ++ctrl+9++). Write your commands, then click the Execute (Do) button or press ++ctrl+d++ to run the entire file. Always begin your do-file with:

* ECON207 Labour Economics — Assignment X
* Author: Your Name
* Date: YYYY-MM-DD
* -----------------------------------------------

clear all
set more off
cap log close
log using "assignment_X.log", replace

And end with:

log close

This creates a complete record of your work.

docs.title: Data Management
docs.text:
These commands form the backbone of every Stata workflow. You will use them in every assignment.

Loading and inspecting data

* Load a Stata dataset
use "plfs_2024_person.dta", clear

* Describe variables (names, types, labels)
describe

* Quick summary statistics
summarize age wage hours_worked

* Detailed summary with percentiles
summarize wage, detail

* Frequency table
tabulate education_level

* Two-way cross-tabulation
tabulate gender employment_status

Creating and modifying variables

* Generate a new variable
gen log_wage = ln(wage)

* Generate a dummy variable
gen female = (gender == 2)

* Generate experience and its square
gen exper = age - education_years - 6
gen exper_sq = exper^2

* Replace values conditionally
replace sector = "Informal" if contract_type == 0

* Keep only relevant observations
keep if age >= 15 & age <= 65

* Drop variables you do not need
drop temp_var1 temp_var2

* Label your variables
label variable log_wage "Log of monthly wage (Rs.)"
label variable female "Female (=1)"

docs.title: Descriptive Statistics and Visualisation
docs.text:
Before running regressions, always explore your data visually and numerically.

Summary statistics and tables

* Mean wage by gender
tabstat wage, by(gender) stat(mean sd n)

* Mean and standard error (useful for reporting)
mean wage, over(gender)

* Detailed tabulation with percentages
tab education_level gender, row col

Graphs for labour economics

* Histogram of log wages
histogram log_wage, ///
    title("Distribution of Log Wages") ///
    xtitle("Log Monthly Wage") ///
    color(navy%70) ///
    normal

* Bar chart of LFPR by education and gender
graph bar (mean) in_labour_force, ///
    over(education_level) over(gender) ///
    title("Labour Force Participation Rate") ///
    ytitle("Proportion in Labour Force") ///
    legend(order(1 "Male" 2 "Female"))

* Scatter plot with fitted line
twoway (scatter log_wage exper, msize(tiny) mcolor(navy%30)) ///
       (lfit log_wage exper, lcolor(red) lwidth(medthick)), ///
    title("Experience-Earnings Profile") ///
    xtitle("Years of Experience") ///
    ytitle("Log Wage")

* Export graphs for your assignment
graph export "wage_histogram.png", replace width(1200)

docs.title: Regression Analysis
docs.text:
Regression is the workhorse of empirical labour economics. The commands below cover the regressions you will encounter in ECON207.

OLS regression -- the Mincer equation (Ch. 6)

* Basic Mincer earnings function
regress log_wage education_years exper exper_sq

* With robust standard errors (always use these)
regress log_wage education_years exper exper_sq, robust

* Adding controls
regress log_wage education_years exper exper_sq female urban, robust

* Interpret: the coefficient on education_years is the
* approximate rate of return to one additional year of schooling

* Store results for comparison
estimates store model1

Instrumental variables -- addressing ability bias (Ch. 6)

* Two-stage least squares (2SLS)
* Instrument: quarter of birth, distance to college, etc.
ivregress 2sls log_wage exper exper_sq (education_years = distance_college), robust

* First-stage diagnostics
estat firststage

* Overidentification test (if multiple instruments)
estat overid

Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition (Ch. 9)

* Install the user-written oaxaca command (one time only)
ssc install oaxaca

* Decompose the male-female wage gap
oaxaca log_wage education_years exper exper_sq urban, ///
    by(female) robust

* Interpret:
* "Explained" = portion due to differences in characteristics
* "Unexplained" = portion due to differences in coefficients
*   (may reflect discrimination + unobserved factors)

docs.title: Labour-Specific Analyses
docs.text:
These examples connect directly to the topics in each chapter.

Labour force participation tabulations (Ch. 2)

* LFPR by age group and gender
gen age_group = .
replace age_group = 1 if age >= 15 & age <= 24
replace age_group = 2 if age >= 25 & age <= 54
replace age_group = 3 if age >= 55 & age <= 65
label define age_lbl 1 "15-24" 2 "25-54" 3 "55-65"
label values age_group age_lbl

tab age_group in_labour_force if gender == 1 [aw=weight], row
tab age_group in_labour_force if gender == 2 [aw=weight], row

Wage equation with compensating differentials (Ch. 5)

* Hedonic wage regression
regress log_wage education_years exper exper_sq ///
    hazardous_job night_shift outdoor_work, robust

* The coefficient on hazardous_job estimates the
* compensating differential for risky work

Unemployment duration analysis (Ch. 11)

* Summarise unemployment duration
summarize unemp_duration if unemployed == 1, detail

* Kaplan-Meier survival curve (if panel data available)
* stset unemp_duration, failure(found_job)
* sts graph, title("Survival in Unemployment")

docs.title: Working with PLFS Data in Stata
docs.text:
The Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) is India's primary labour market dataset. For the group assignments, you will use cleaned PLFS microdata in .dta format.

Loading PLFS data

* Set your working directory
cd "/path/to/your/data/"

* Load the person-level file
use "plfs_2024_person.dta", clear

* Inspect the dataset
describe
summarize

docs.title: Key PLFS Variables
docs.text:
Variable Description Notes age Age in years Working age: 15+ sex Sex (1=Male, 2=Female) sector Rural (1) / Urban (2) nss_region NSS region code For regional analysis usual_status Usual principal activity status 11-51 = employed; 81 = unemployed; 91-97 = NILF current_weekly_status CWS activity status More current measure nco_2d 2-digit NCO occupation code For occupation-level analysis nic_2d 2-digit NIC industry code For industry-level analysis education Highest education level General education categories wage_salary Wage/salary earnings Available for regular and casual workers weight Sampling weight (multiplier) Always use weights for population estimates

Weighted estimates

* IMPORTANT: Always use sampling weights for population-level statistics

* Weighted mean
mean wage_salary [pw=weight]

* Weighted tabulation
tab education sex [aw=weight], row

* Weighted regression
regress log_wage education_years exper exper_sq [pw=weight], robust

PLFS Activity Status Codes

The PLFS uses a detailed activity classification. The key codes for labour force status are:

  • 11-51: Employed (self-employed, regular wage, casual)
  • 81: Unemployed (seeking/available for work)
  • 91-97: Not in labour force (student, domestic duties, rentier, etc.)

To construct the labour force dummy:

gen in_lf = (usual_status >= 11 & usual_status <= 82)
gen employed = (usual_status >= 11 & usual_status <= 51)
gen unemployed = (usual_status == 81)

docs.title: Tips for Assignments
docs.text:
1. Always use a do-file. Never run commands only in the Command window. Your do-file is your submission.
  2. Comment your code generously. Use * for full-line comments and // for inline comments.
  3. Use robust standard errors in all regressions unless instructed otherwise.
  4. Always use sampling weights when computing population-level statistics from PLFS data.
  5. Export tables and graphs in publication-ready format. Use esttab (from the estout package) for regression tables and graph export for figures.
  6. Reproduce before you extend. First replicate the textbook result, then add the Indian context.

Installing useful packages

* Run these once to install commonly needed commands
ssc install estout      // For publication-quality tables
ssc install oaxaca      // Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition
ssc install coefplot    // Coefficient plots
ssc install binscatter  // Binned scatter plots
